definition: Selling an action's power and exertion by extending its RECOVERY (the vulnerable window after the effect lands) rather than its anticipation/wind-up, when a responsive player action cannot afford a long startup.
purpose: Preserve near-instantaneous input responsiveness on a player-controlled action while still communicating that the action is powerful and costly, by moving the "this takes real effort" signal to after the hit instead of before it.
visible_effect: A near-instant transition from idle to the effect-connecting frame (little or no visible wind-up), followed by a comparatively long hold, stagger, or slow return-to-idle after the action lands.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Preserves the feel of an immediately-responsive control scheme while still reading as a heavy, costly action; as a side effect, creates a player-facing risk/reward decision (a longer recovery leaves the player vulnerable for longer), which a short anticipation-based wind-up does not.
physical_interpretation: Not a substitute for real physicality in the anticipation sense — the video is explicit that this is a game-feel trick, not a physically accurate stand-in for a proper wind-up.
use_cases: a player-controlled action in a genre where responsiveness is the priority (most action games' core moveset)
a design that wants a deliberate risk/reward tradeoff on powerful moves — commit to a big hit, pay for it in exposed recovery time
any move where anticipation time has already been minimized for feel and further power communication is still needed
non_use_cases: a non-player-controlled action (an enemy or environmental hazard), where anticipation time exists specifically so the PLAYER can react to it — recovery time serves the acting character's own risk, not the opponent's ability to read the attack coming

a genre where responsiveness is not the binding constraint in the first place (turn-based, RTS, or other non-directly-controlled contexts), where ordinary anticipation is simply affordable and this substitution is unnecessary
treating this as free — it still costs the player time and exposure, just after the hit rather than before it
interactions: Anticipation — explicitly a substitute for it, trading WHERE the "this costs something" signal sits in the timeline, not eliminating the cost
Startup frame budget — the same responsiveness pressure that pins startup low is exactly what motivates shifting the weight-selling job to recovery instead
Timing — a pure relative-duration decision: recovery duration versus startup duration for the same total "this move is costly" budget

style_variations.game_combat: the primary context this technique exists for; a purely non-interactive medium (film, a cutscene) has no reason to prefer recovery over anticipation, since nothing is waiting on a player input

cadence_representation: Not represented as a named tradeoff. The underlying editable quantity is ordinary phase timing — lengthening the keys/hold after a contact marker versus before it — fully reachable through existing key placement and `ai/events.js` markers, but nothing frames "recovery duration" as an alternative lever to "anticipation duration" for the same design goal the way this entry does.
control_surface: Indirect, through ordinary key/marker placement after a contact event; no vocabulary dimension distinguishes recovery-as-weight-signal from any other post-contact motion.
detection_and_measurement_methods: Real and directly available: the duration from a contact/impact marker to the next actionable/idle state is exactly as measurable as startup duration is (same marker-to-marker distance computation, the other direction) — `ai/events.js` and existing key timestamps already carry what is needed; nothing currently reports it as its own named quantity.
generation_or_modification_methods: None dedicated. Extending recovery today means moving or adding keys after the contact point directly; no strategy trades startup budget for recovery budget as a single declared decision.
failure_modes: applying long recovery to a non-player character's attack, where the player needed anticipation time to react and a long recovery afterward does not help them read the attack coming in the first place
recovery so long it stops feeling like weight and starts feeling like unresponsive lag, the same failure slow_in_slow_out already names for an overused ease
using this as a free substitute rather than acknowledging it still costs the player something — exposure time — which needs to be balanced like any other risk/reward lever
roblox_considerations: None specific — a pure keyframe-timing/game-design concept independent of the target engine.
examples: a player character's powerful attack connecting almost immediately on input, then leaving them momentarily unable to act while recovering — named directly as a common strategy for selling power without costing anticipation time (video 3 @ 5:16–5:44)
the same design also cited as a deliberate risk/reward lever: a more powerful move leaves the player vulnerable for longer afterward, as a built-in cost for its strength (video 3 @ 5:40–5:44)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/28s1Hv3Zqlo @ 5:16–5:44 — Dan states the technique and its risk/reward design consequence directly, over generic gameplay b-roll rather than one named, identifiable example; experimental until validated
